title: Choose a Cato
hook: pick someone good and live as if they were watching

segments.voice: Yesterday: Athenodorus, one self instead of two, and your line, the private and public self become one. Did you act once, alone, as if someone kind were watching? Day four hundred forty-five.

When you're stuck on something, a hard conversation, a temptation, a choice at work, there's a question people reach for: what would she do? My grandmother. My old coach. The best boss I ever had. Some people keep a name on a bracelet for just that moment. The move is old. Yesterday Seneca said to live as if God saw you. In his eleventh letter he makes it more human and more specific, with advice he borrows, once again, from Epicurus. Today: choose a Cato.
screen: `WHAT WOULD SHE DO?` → `A NAME ON A BRACELET.` → `CHOOSE A CATO.`

segments.voice: First, the blush. The letter starts with a young friend of Lucilius who blushed while talking to Seneca. Seneca liked him for it. Blushing, he says, is natural, and no amount of wisdom removes it. Actors can fake tears or fear on stage, but they can't blush on command. Some things in us we can't control; character is about what we do with the rest. Second, the guardian. Then the advice. Epicurus, Seneca says, told his students to pick out a person of good character and keep them always before their eyes, living as if that person were watching and acting as if that person could see. A guardian, Seneca calls it, a witness you carry with you. Third, the names. Choose a Cato, Seneca says. Cato the Younger was the stern Roman Stoic who refused to bend to Julius Caesar and died rather than submit. If Cato feels too severe, Seneca adds, choose Laelius, a gentler man, a statesman known as the Wise. Choose someone whose life and words and even face have pleased you. Fourth, the ruler. Why does it work? Because, Seneca says, you can't straighten something crooked without a ruler. We need a measure outside ourselves to see where we bend. Your Cato doesn't have to be famous, or Roman, or even alive. It can be a grandmother, a saint, a teacher, a neighbor. It just has to be someone whose goodness you're sure of, and whose imagined gaze makes you stand a little straighter.
screen: `THE BLUSH NO WISDOM REMOVES.` · `KEEP A GOOD PERSON BEFORE YOU.` · `CATO, OR GENTLER LAELIUS.` · `NO STRAIGHT LINE WITHOUT A RULER.` · then, large: `CHOOSE A CATO.`

segments.voice: Let your breath settle. Now let faces come to mind, people whose goodness you trust. Living or gone. Famous or known only to you. Don't pick yet, just let them come. Then let one step forward. That's your Cato. Recall one thing you actually saw them do, or know they did: a small, straight act. Hold it up like a ruler next to one choice you're facing this week. Where does your line bend away from theirs? No scolding. Just measure. The bell holds the time.
Cato. Seneca's eleventh letter, borrowing from Epicurus: choose someone good and live as if they were watching, a ruler to straighten yourself against. Today's word.
Your line: stand a little straighter. Keep the watcher you picked with you today. At one decision, ask what they'd see, and let that be your ruler. Day four hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism keep a chosen model in mind, a person of good character, and ask in hard moments what that person would see in their choices.

original.note: Latin: so choose a Cato, from Seneca's eleventh letter.

trapdoor: what you thought: find a role model.
what it means: Seneca, borrowing from Epicurus, says keep a good person before your eyes as a watcher and a ruler to straighten yourself against.
what a scholar hears: Seneca's word for the watcher is custos, a guardian, and he takes the idea from Epicurus, a rival school, without apology.
recall: the Stoic Seneca calls our Hecaton

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: practice rewritten so it no longer repeats day 444's imagined kind gaze (now a ruler: measure one choice against one remembered act); garbled bracelet line fixed; Utica date and 'favorite example' superlative removed from trapdoor.

Letter 11.1–7: the young man who blushed; blushing not removed by wisdom; actors cannot blush at will. 11.8–10: Epicurus' advice to keep a good man before one's eyes as guardian (custos); 'elige itaque Catonem'; or Laelius, of gentler spirit; the ruler (regula) that straightens the crooked. Paraphrased; confirm.
Cato the Younger's death at Utica, 46 BCE, after Thapsus; Laelius as 'Sapiens' (Gaius Laelius, friend of Scipio Aemilianus). Confirm.
